title: Queens Govern Siruguppa and Naregal
subtitle: Queens of Record, Queens of Rule
era: Women and administration under Vikramaditya VI, late 11th-early 12th century CE
region: Siruguppa, Naregal, Kalyani and the western Deccan
moral: Power also lives in records that name those who governed.

sources.citation: Vikramaditya VI-period inscriptions naming Kethala Devi at Siruguppa and Savala Devi at Naregal
sources.note: Primary evidence for female administrative roles.

sources.citation: Chandala Devi references in Chalukya records as Abhinava Saraswati
sources.note: Evidence for elite women in cultural patronage.

sources.citation: B.R. Gopal, The Chalukyas of Kalyani (1981); Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice (2001)
sources.note: Modern frameworks for reading inscriptions as social and administrative evidence.

panels.shot: epic split composition, half Siruguppa, half Naregal, with both queens in regal profile

dialogue.text: In Vikramaditya VI’s glittering age, two Chalukya queens—Kethala Devi of Siruguppa and Savala Devi of Naregal—step out of shadow, not in legend, but in stone records of rule.

panels.shot: slow push-in on an ancient inscription slab half-buried in soil

dialogue.text: Centuries later, it is not a court poet but a carved stone in Siruguppa that first whispers Kethala Devi’s name—and calls her administrator of this land.

panels.shot: wide aerial of the western Deccan under soft dawn light

dialogue.text: This is Vikramaditya VI’s Deccan, late 11th century. The Chalukyas of Kalyani hold sway, their power stitched together by land grants, courts of law, and a web of local chiefs.

panels.shot: majestic wide shot of Kalyani court interior

dialogue.text: In Kalyani’s royal court, grants are issued, taxes ordered, scholars honoured. Here, Vikramaditya VI signs his name into history—yet on many records, a queen’s name stands beside his.

panels.shot: medium shot of both queens seated slightly behind the throne, observing

dialogue.text: Tradition paints queens as distant consorts. But the inscriptions of this reign—read closely by modern historians—show some royal women woven into the machinery of rule.

panels.shot: close-up on Kethala Devi’s steady face, Savala Devi slightly blurred in background

dialogue.text: Kethala Devi’s Siruguppa is a tract of fields and villages along the Tungabhadra. Her name in inscriptions marks her as the authority over its revenue and its obligations.

panels.shot: wide village scene in Siruguppa, queen overseeing officials

dialogue.text: Under the king’s overarching sovereignty, Siruguppa must deliver grain, coin and loyalty. The inscription places Kethala Devi between palace and plough—responsible that dues are levied and grants enforced.

panels.shot: medium shot of Savala Devi in Naregal amidst temple and houses

dialogue.text: Far to the west at Naregal, Savala Devi appears in another record, tied to an agrahara—a Brahmin settlement endowed with land, tax privileges and the duty to keep learning alive.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of Savala Devi with Brahmin elders and scribes

dialogue.text: The Naregal inscription names her in the formal language of donation and administration. Through her, land is assigned, taxes remitted, and a small world of scholars anchored in place.

panels.shot: close-up of a stylus etching characters onto palm leaf, queens’ hands nearby

dialogue.text: Each line of such records has weight. When a queen’s name appears in the chain of responsibility, it signals more than ceremony—it ties her to the legal fabric of that place.

panels.shot: wide composite shot of courtroom scene and rural tax collection

dialogue.text: Still, power is not evenly shared. These records speak of elite women in royal circles, not of ordinary women voting or ruling. Authority flows along narrow family lines.

panels.shot: medium shot of both queens in a quiet corridor, partially in shadow

dialogue.text: Modern scholars like B.R. Gopal and Cynthia Talbot sift these stones carefully. They see in them real administrative agency—yet warn against turning a handful of queens into a picture of full equality.

panels.shot: majestic wide shot of Chandala Devi in a hall of music and manuscripts

dialogue.text: Another woman of this age, Chandala Devi, is praised in records as Abhinava Saraswati—‘a new Saraswati’—for her patronage of learning and the arts, a different face of power.

panels.shot: close-up on Chandala Devi listening to a poet, queens faintly in background montage

dialogue.text: Queens could shape courts through patronage or through office. In each case, the inscription fixes their contribution—be it a village for scholars or a tract under their charge.

panels.shot: somber wide shot of later Chalukya territory fracturing

dialogue.text: Even as Vikramaditya VI’s reign shines, strains deepen. After him, the Later Chalukya hold frays, rivals rise, and new powers claim the land these queens once helped manage.

panels.shot: quiet close-up of an inscription weathering under rain, queens fading into stone

dialogue.text: Dynasties fall. Villages change hands. But a few slabs endure, their worn letters still spelling out names like Kethala Devi and Savala Devi where once only kings were expected.

panels.shot: modern historian’s study with inscription rubbings pinned on walls

dialogue.text: Today, gender-focused readings of such records recover these women from footnotes. They do not stretch the evidence; they simply follow the lines that the stone already carries.

panels.shot: epic low-angle of both queens standing tall against a backdrop of inscribed stone slabs

dialogue.text: Their rule did not overturn the old order. Yet their recorded presence unsettles easy stories—reminding us that power’s trace is also in which names records choose to speak aloud.
